newsitem.title: USA: Warmer reception seen for US 10-yr notes than 3-yr.
newsitem.headline: Warmer reception seen for US 10-yr notes than 3-yr.

text.p: After a less-than-enthusiastic reception for the U.S. Treasury's sale of three-year notes on Tuesday, traders said they expected a somewhat warmer greeting for Wednesday's 10-year note auction.

As part of its quarterly refunding, the Treasury is slated to sell $12 billion in 10-year notes at 1300 EST/1800 GMT, sandwiched between Tuesday's $17.75 billion three-year note auction and Thursday's $10 million 30-year bond sale.

"It has been one of the quietest refundings around," observed Mead Briggs, head of proprietary U.S. government bond trading at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "Nobody cared about the three-years and there's only a little more talk about caring on the 10-years."
Around 1130 EST/1630 GMT, the when-issued 10-year note was trading at 6.38 percent, virtually unchanged from late Tuesday and 1.5 basis points lower than from the start of trading in the U.S.

"There is a lot of interest in the 10-year auction," said Christopher Fitzmaurice, a 10-year note trader at Salomon Brothers Inc. "It is a smaller size than the previous two (10-year) auctions and (the notes) are cheap to mortgages and European government bonds."
He noted that there should be "real retail interest" above 6.40 percent.
"Realistically, we should see them close to that level," Briggs said. "They have nice value around 6.45 percent but that's not realistic for this auction."

Briggs noted that the auction should go fairly well because with the Federal Reserve seemingly on hold, "bullish people say the curve is flattening and want longer paper, either outright or on spread."

Plus, he added, with more 10-year corporate paper, traders will use the issue as a hedge against corporates, which creates a good bid in the repo market, thereby making them even Still, Briggs and others said some players might not want to bid on the new notes ahead of Thursday's release of January retail sales data, seen up 0.7 percent.

"There is a lot of fear, uncertainty and apathy toward Treasuries ahead of retail sales," he said. "The market is going nowhere. The price action and volumes are indicating nothing is going on. That may all change ... but that's what it looks like now."
According to GovPX, which tracks volume, trading in the when-issued 10-year note totaled about $440 million, compared with $2.12 billion in the outstanding 10-year note.
Overall Treasury market volume at 1130 EST/1630 GMT was about $36 billion, with activity concentrated largely in short- and intermediate coupons.
